standard_prerequisites.name: Non-degenerate interval exchange transformation
standard_prerequisites.statement: An IET given by a permutation and a length vector, with all continuity intervals of positive length.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the object of the statement.

standard_prerequisites.name: Conjugacy equation
standard_prerequisites.statement: The reflection of the interval conjugates the transformation to its inverse off the discontinuities.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the hypothesis of the statement.

standard_prerequisites.name: Order on intervals
standard_prerequisites.statement: One interval is below another when every point of the first is below every point of the second.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the order that the argument shows is reversed both by the transformation and by the reflection.

core_obligations: Order the continuity intervals by decreasing length, so that the longest one is distinguished, and observe that the conjugate of the transformation is continuous on its interior (source lines 497-498).

Show that the reflection of the longest interval equals its image under the transformation, by comparing where both sides can be discontinuous and using the hypothesis that the lengths are pairwise distinct (source lines 498-501).
Extend that identity to every continuity interval by induction on the position in the decreasing order (source line 503).

Use that the reflection reverses the order defined on intervals while the transformation reverses it as well, given the identity just proved, to conclude that the permutation is symmetric (source lines 503-507).

proof_roadmap.step: Establish the reflection identity for the longest continuity interval.
Propagate the identity to all continuity intervals by induction on length.
Compare the order reversal of the reflection with that of the transformation to obtain symmetry.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 489-494: a non-degenerate interval exchange transformation that satisfies the conjugacy equation and whose continuity intervals have pairwise distinct lengths is symmetric. The proof (source lines 496-508) is an induction that is not visible in the statement: the continuity intervals are first ordered by decreasing length, so that the longest one is singled out; the reflection identity is proved for that one by comparing the possible discontinuities of the two sides, and the hypothesis that the lengths are pairwise distinct is what makes that comparison conclusive; the identity is then propagated along the decreasing order, after which the reversal of the order by the reflection and by the transformation gives the symmetry of the permutation.
